cat accessor.summary: `Series.cat` provides access to categorical properties and operations. In a DataFrame workflow, select a categorical column and use `.cat` on the resulting Series.
cat accessor.explanation: The `cat` accessor exposes categorical properties and operations for a Series whose values use pandas' categorical dtype. Access it through a categorical DataFrame column, then call accessor attributes or methods such as `categories` and `codes`.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: The Series or CategoricalIndex to which the categorical accessor is attached.

cat accessor.returns: An accessor object for categorical properties of the Series values.

example.title: Inspect categorical column metadata
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"animal": ["cat", "dog", "cat"]})
df["animal"] = df["animal"].astype("category")
print(df["animal"].cat.categories.tolist())
print(df["animal"].cat.codes.tolist())
example.explanation: Convert a column to categorical data, then inspect its categories and integer codes.

useCases.title: Read category metadata
useCases.scenario: Inspect the distinct labels and internal integer representation of a categorical DataFrame column.

useCases.title: Manipulate categories
useCases.scenario: Apply category-level transformations to a selected DataFrame column.

useCases.title: Process categorical DataFrame data
useCases.scenario: Work with categorical columns while retaining pandas indexing and slicing behavior.

interview.question: What does the pandas `cat` accessor provide?
interview.answer: `cat` is an accessor for categorical properties of Series values. For a DataFrame, select a categorical column first, for example `df["animal"].cat.categories`.
interview.followUp: How would you make a non-categorical column usable with `cat`? Convert it with `astype("category")` or assign a categorical dtype.

interview.question: How do you expose `cat` from a DataFrame?
interview.answer: A DataFrame column can be categorical when constructed with `dtype="category"` or converted afterward. Selecting that column returns a Series on which the accessor is available.
interview.followUp: What must be preserved when assigning categorical values? The assigned values must already belong to the column's categories.

interview.question: Is `cat` a DataFrame-wide accessor?
interview.answer: The accessor exposes categorical metadata and transformations, including category labels and category codes. Operations are performed on the Series selected from the DataFrame rather than directly on the DataFrame object.
interview.followUp: What happens if a row selection changes the result to a non-categorical Series? The category dtype may not be preserved for a single-row result, so the accessor may no longer be available.

keyPoints: `cat` is an accessor object for categorical properties.
A DataFrame column can carry categorical data, making it the usual entry point for using `cat` in DataFrame workflows.
Use the categorical dtype during construction when creating categorical data from the start.
Standard DataFrame indexing methods continue to work with categorical columns.
Assignments to categorical data are restricted to values already listed in its categories.
Slicing that returns a DataFrame or a column Series preserves the categorical dtype.
gotchas: `cat` applies to categorical Series values; a regular object- or string-typed column must first be converted to categorical dtype.
Other accessors depend on the types of the categories, so categorical data does not automatically make every accessor operation valid.

DataFrame.summary: A DataFrame is pandas’ mutable, two-dimensional table with labeled rows and columns. Its columns can hold different data types, and arithmetic aligns values by both axis labels.
DataFrame.explanation: DataFrame constructs a mutable two-dimensional table whose rows and columns have labels and whose columns may hold different data types. Operations use those labels for alignment, while indexing tools such as loc and iloc select data by labels or integer positions.
DataFrame.syntax: class pandas.DataFrame(data=None, index=None, columns=None, dtype=None, copy=None)

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Initial table data.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: Row labels.

parameters.name: columns
parameters.description: Column labels.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Data type to use when constructing the table.

parameters.name: copy
parameters.description: Whether to copy input data.

example.title: Create and select a DataFrame
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"name": ["Ada", "Linus"], "score": [98, 87]},
    index=["a", "b"],
)
df["passed"] = df["score"] >= 90
print(df.loc[df["passed"], ["name", "score"]])
example.explanation: Creates a labeled table from column data, derives a Boolean column, and selects rows and columns by labels.

useCases.title: Build tabular datasets
useCases.scenario: Represent records with named fields and stable row labels.

useCases.title: Filter and project data
useCases.scenario: Keep only rows satisfying a condition and choose selected fields.

useCases.title: Label-aware transformations
useCases.scenario: Combine or calculate tables while preserving meaningful row and column labels.

interview.question: What is a pandas DataFrame?
interview.answer: DataFrame is pandas' primary two-dimensional data structure. It is size-mutable, can contain heterogeneous column types, and has labeled row and column axes.
interview.followUp: How are arithmetic operations matched? They align values on both row and column labels rather than relying only on physical position.

interview.question: What does the DataFrame constructor accept?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts data plus optional index, columns, dtype, and copy arguments. Data can therefore be shaped and labeled explicitly when the table is created.
interview.followUp: Which constructor argument controls the row labels? The index argument supplies them; columns supplies the column labels.

interview.question: How do loc and iloc differ?
interview.answer: loc selects by label or Boolean array, whereas iloc selects by integer position. Use loc when axis labels define the selection and iloc when positions define it.
interview.followUp: How would you select one cell by each style? Use at for a single row/column label pair and iat for a single integer-position pair.

keyPoints: Use DataFrame for a table that can grow or change and whose columns may have different value types.
Rows and columns carry labels, enabling selections and operations that refer to meaningful axis names.
Many pandas workflows use DataFrame as the central object for tabular data manipulation.
Construct a table with optional source data, axis labels, a dtype, and copying behavior.
Use loc for label-based or Boolean filtering across rows and columns.
Use iloc when the desired rows or columns are specified by zero-based positions.
gotchas: Arithmetic combines values according to matching row and column labels, so differently ordered or named axes can affect results.
Treating columns like dictionary entries is useful, but it does not make the object an ordinary dictionary; DataFrame indexing and axis behavior still apply.

df.agg.summary: DataFrame.agg applies one or more aggregation operations over a selected axis. It supports single operations, lists of operations, per-column dictionaries, and named aggregations.
df.agg.explanation: DataFrame.agg applies one or more aggregation operations along a chosen axis. Pass a callable or operation name, a list for multiple operations, or a dictionary to specify operations by column; additional positional and keyword arguments are forwarded to the aggregation function.

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function, string, list, or dictionary specifying the operation or operations used for aggregation.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis over which to aggregate: 0 or index for columns, or 1 or columns for rows. Defaults to 0.

parameters.name: *args
parameters.description: Additional positional arguments passed to the aggregation function.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.description: Additional keyword arguments passed to the aggregation function.

df.agg.returns: scalar, Series or DataFrame, depending on the object and aggregation specification.

example.title: Aggregate columns with different operations
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 4, 7], "B": [2, 5, 8]})
result = df.agg({"A": ["sum", "min"], "B": "mean"})
print(result)
example.explanation: Computes multiple aggregations for column A and the mean for column B.

useCases.title: Column summaries
useCases.scenario: You need totals, extrema, or averages for every column in one operation.

useCases.title: Per-column aggregation
useCases.scenario: Different columns require different reductions, such as sum for one and mean for another.

useCases.title: Multiple reductions
useCases.scenario: You need several statistics for each column, such as sum and minimum.

useCases.title: Row-wise aggregation
useCases.scenario: You want a row-level statistic across columns.

interview.question: What does the axis argument control?
interview.answer: By default, agg uses axis=0, so each function is applied to every column. Set axis=1 or axis="columns" to aggregate across each row instead.
interview.followUp: What result shape should you expect from several functions? A DataFrame is returned, with aggregation names represented in the result index when aggregating columns.

interview.question: Which forms can func take?
interview.answer: func can be a callable, a string naming an operation, a list of operations, or a dictionary mapping columns to operations. A list requests multiple aggregations, while a dictionary allows different operations for different columns.
interview.followUp: How would you combine named results? Use named aggregation keyword arguments such as x=("A", "max") and y=("B", "min").

interview.question: What can DataFrame.agg return?
interview.answer: For DataFrame.agg, a single aggregation generally produces a Series, while multiple aggregations produce a DataFrame. The documented return possibilities are scalar, Series, or DataFrame depending on the object and aggregation used.
interview.followUp: What is the related method name? aggregate is an alias for agg, so either spelling invokes the same operation.

keyPoints: Use agg when you need one or several reductions, such as sum, mean, or min, over a DataFrame axis.
The func argument identifies the aggregation and may be a callable, operation name, list, or column-to-operation mapping.
The default axis=0 reduces each column independently and returns results aligned to the column labels.
Use axis=1, or the equivalent columns label, to calculate an aggregation separately for every row.
Every aggregation has an explicit direction: across the index for column-wise work or across columns for row-wise work.
aggregate is the longer equivalent spelling, so code can use either DataFrame.agg or DataFrame.aggregate.
gotchas: A callable must accept the DataFrame itself or be usable by DataFrame.apply; functions designed only for individual scalar values may not work as expected.

df.apply.summary: Apply a callable independently along each DataFrame column or row. The default passes labeled Series objects and infers the result shape from the callable; options support ndarray inputs and explicit row-wise list-result handling.
df.apply.explanation: DataFrame.apply runs a callable across columns or rows. By default it passes each selected axis as a Series and infers the output structure from the callable's result; options can instead pass arrays or control list-like row results.
df.apply.syntax: DataFrame.apply(func, axis=0, raw=False, result_type=None, args=(), by_row='compat', engine=None, engine_kwargs=None, **kwargs)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function to apply to each column or row.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis to process: 0 or 'index' for columns; 1 or 'columns' for rows. Default is 0.

parameters.name: raw
parameters.description: Whether to pass ndarray objects instead of Series objects. Default is False.

parameters.name: result_type
parameters.description: How to interpret list-like row results: 'expand', 'reduce', 'broadcast', or None. Default is None.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Additional positional arguments passed to func.

parameters.name: by_row
parameters.description: Controls row-wise compatibility handling for list-like or dict-like callables. Default is 'compat'.

parameters.name: engine
parameters.description: Execution engine selection. Default is None.

parameters.name: engine_kwargs
parameters.description: Additional keyword arguments for the selected engine.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.description: Additional keyword arguments passed to func.

df.apply.returns: Series or DataFrame: Result of applying func along the given axis of the DataFrame.

example.title: Apply a function to columns and rows
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [10, 20]})
column_totals = df.apply(sum)
row_totals = df.apply(sum, axis="columns")
print(column_totals.to_dict())
print(row_totals.tolist())
example.explanation: Applies the callable once to each column by default, then once to each row when the column axis is selected.

useCases.title: Column-wise calculations
useCases.scenario: Compute per-column summaries such as totals, ranges, or custom statistics.

useCases.title: Row-wise feature creation
useCases.scenario: Derive a value from multiple fields in each record.

useCases.title: Controlling row-result shape
useCases.scenario: Turn each row's list-like result into columns or retain the original shape.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.apply do, and what is the default axis?
interview.answer: It applies a function along one DataFrame axis and returns a Series or DataFrame. With axis=0, the function receives each column; with axis=1, it receives each row.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the original shape for row-wise list-like output? Use result_type='broadcast', which broadcasts results to the original DataFrame shape and retains its index and columns.

interview.question: How do raw and result_type affect apply?
interview.answer: raw=False is the default, so the callable receives each row or column as a Series. With raw=True, it receives an ndarray instead, which can avoid Series-specific overhead.
interview.followUp: When does result_type matter? It controls list-like results only for axis=1, with expand, reduce, or broadcast determining the resulting shape.

interview.question: Which arguments let you configure the callable and execution?
interview.answer: The callable can be passed positional arguments through args and keyword arguments through kwargs. The by_row option controls how list-like or dict-like callables are handled when applying row-wise compatibility behavior.
interview.followUp: What does the engine option represent? The current signature allows an engine selection and engine_kwargs for execution-specific configuration; consult the documented engine choices before relying on them.

keyPoints: func is the callable invoked for every selected column or row.
The default axis=0 processes columns; axis='columns' or axis=1 processes rows.
With raw=False, each input is a labeled Series, while raw=True supplies an ndarray.
For row-wise application, result_type='expand' converts list-like outputs into separate columns.
For row-wise list-like results, reduce favors a Series instead of expanding them into columns.
The broadcast mode keeps the DataFrame's original shape, index, and columns when compatible.
gotchas: result_type has an effect only for row-wise application; setting it while applying by column does not change the result.
When outputs vary across rows or columns, the first result can determine the inferred result structure, so return consistently shaped values.
Do not assume a DataFrame or Series result; inspect the callable's output and choose result_type when row-wise shape needs to be explicit.

df.applymap.summary: DataFrame.applymap applies a scalar-to-scalar callable to every DataFrame element and returns a transformed DataFrame. It is deprecated; use DataFrame.map instead.
df.applymap.explanation: DataFrame.applymap applies a callable separately to every DataFrame element. The callable must accept one scalar and return one scalar; optional keyword arguments are forwarded to it, while na_action='ignore' preserves missing values without calling the function.

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Callable receiving one DataFrame element and returning one value.

parameters.name: na_action
parameters.description: Controls missing-value handling; 'ignore' propagates missing values without calling func.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.description: Additional keyword arguments passed to func.

example.title: Elementwise transformation
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
result = df.applymap(lambda value: value * 10)
print(result)
example.explanation: Creates a new DataFrame by multiplying each cell value by 10.

useCases.title: Elementwise conversion
useCases.scenario: Applying a uniform scalar conversion to every cell in a small or irregular DataFrame.

useCases.title: Missing-value-aware processing
useCases.scenario: Skipping missing values while applying a scalar formatter or validator.

useCases.title: Compatibility migration
useCases.scenario: Maintaining older code temporarily while migrating to the current API.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.applymap do?
interview.answer: It transforms every cell independently and returns a DataFrame. The callable receives one scalar and must return one scalar.
interview.followUp: What should replace it in current pandas? Use DataFrame.map, which is the renamed elementwise DataFrame method.

interview.question: How does na_action affect missing values?
interview.answer: na_action accepts None or 'ignore'. With 'ignore', missing values are propagated and are not passed to the callable.
interview.followUp: Why can this matter? A callable that assumes a concrete value may otherwise receive a missing-value marker.

interview.question: How are extra arguments passed, and what performance concern applies?
interview.answer: The method accepts additional keyword arguments through **kwargs and forwards them to the callable. This allows configuration without wrapping the callable in another function.
interview.followUp: What performance alternative should be considered first? Use a vectorized pandas or NumPy operation when available.

keyPoints: The callable runs independently for each cell rather than along rows or columns.
func must map one scalar input to one scalar output.
Keyword arguments supplied to applymap are forwarded to func.
The method is deprecated in current pandas documentation.
DataFrame.map is the documented replacement for applymap.
gotchas: This method is deprecated; use DataFrame.map for new code.
With na_action='ignore', missing values pass through unchanged and are not given to the callable.
Prefer a vectorized operation when one exists because elementwise Python calls can be slower.

df.assign.summary: DataFrame.assign creates or replaces columns and returns a new DataFrame containing the original columns plus the results. Values may be direct data or callables evaluated against the DataFrame.
df.assign.explanation: DataFrame.assign returns a new DataFrame containing the original columns plus columns named by the keyword arguments. Each value can be computed from the DataFrame with a callable or assigned directly from a Series, scalar, or array-like value; keyword arguments are processed in order.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.type: callable, Series, scalar, array-like, or dict
parameters.description: Column names are keywords. Values may be callable, Series, scalar, or array-like; callables are evaluated with the DataFrame and direct values are assigned.

df.assign.returns: DataFrame: A new DataFrame with the new columns in addition to all the existing columns.

example.title: Create dependent columns
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"temp_c": [17.0, 25.0]})
result = df.assign(
    temp_f=lambda frame: frame["temp_c"] * 9 / 5 + 32,
    label=lambda frame: frame["temp_f"].round(1).astype(str) + " °F",
)

print(result)
example.explanation: Creates two derived columns; the second callable uses the column created earlier in the same assign call.

useCases.title: Add calculated columns
useCases.scenario: Derive measurements or labels from existing columns.

useCases.title: Create dependent columns
useCases.scenario: Build a sequence of transformations where later results use earlier results.

useCases.title: Overwrite columns immutably
useCases.scenario: Replace selected columns while retaining the rest of the DataFrame.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.assign do?
interview.answer: assign accepts keyword arguments whose names become column names. Callable values receive the DataFrame, while non-callable values such as Series, scalars, or arrays are assigned directly. The method returns a new DataFrame rather than modifying the original.
interview.followUp: How can one derived column depend on another created in the same call? Place the dependent expression after the first keyword argument; assignment is evaluated in keyword order.

interview.question: How are multiple columns and name collisions handled?
interview.answer: Multiple columns can be supplied in one assign call. Each keyword names a resulting column, and an existing column with the same name is overwritten in the returned object.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to callable values? They must not mutate the input DataFrame, even though pandas does not check for mutation.

interview.question: Can one assign expression use a column defined earlier in the same call?
interview.answer: Later keyword expressions can refer to columns created or modified earlier in the same call because items are computed and assigned sequentially. This enables concise dependent transformations.
interview.followUp: What happens to the source DataFrame? It remains unchanged because assign returns a new DataFrame containing the added or replaced columns.

keyPoints: Use assign to add named columns through keyword arguments.
The result preserves the source columns and includes the columns supplied to assign.
A callable receives the DataFrame and produces the value for its named output column.
Direct values can be provided without a callable, including Series, scalars, and arrays.
One call can define several columns at once.
Keyword order supports dependent column creation: later expressions can use earlier results.
gotchas: A callable supplied to assign should calculate its result without mutating the input DataFrame; pandas does not enforce this restriction.
Using an existing column name replaces that column in the returned DataFrame.

df.astype.summary: DataFrame.astype casts an entire DataFrame to one dtype or applies dtypes column by column through a mapping. Invalid conversions raise by default, with errors='ignore' available to suppress them.
df.astype.explanation: Call astype with one dtype to convert the whole DataFrame, or pass a column-to-dtype mapping for selective conversion. The method returns a DataFrame with the requested types; invalid conversions raise by default unless errors is set to ignore.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.type: str, data type, Series, or Mapping of column name to data type
parameters.description: Target dtype for the entire object, or a mapping of column names to individual target dtypes. Supported dtype forms include strings, numpy dtypes, pandas extension dtypes, Python types, and Series.

parameters.name: copy
parameters.description: Whether to copy data when performing the conversion. The current documentation signature uses a no-default sentinel.

parameters.name: errors
parameters.description: Controls exception handling for invalid data: raise exceptions or suppress them.

example.title: Cast selected columns
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"count": [1, 2], "score": [3, 4]})
converted = df.astype({"count": "int32", "score": "float32"})
print(converted.dtypes)
example.explanation: A mapping applies a separate target dtype to each named column.

useCases.title: Whole-DataFrame type normalization
useCases.scenario: Normalize every column to a shared numeric or string representation before downstream processing.

useCases.title: Per-column conversion
useCases.scenario: Convert selected columns to different numeric widths or other target dtypes while preserving unmapped columns.

useCases.title: Tolerant conversion
useCases.scenario: Attempt a best-effort conversion in a pipeline where invalid values should not immediately abort processing.

interview.question: How do you use astype for whole-frame and per-column conversion?
interview.answer: Pass a single dtype such as 'int32' to cast the entire DataFrame, or pass a mapping from column labels to dtypes to cast selected columns independently. The mapping can target one or more columns.
interview.followUp: How can failed conversions be suppressed? Set errors='ignore'; the documentation defines this option as suppressing exceptions for invalid data.

interview.question: What forms can the dtype argument take?
interview.answer: dtype accepts a string, numpy dtype, pandas extension dtype, Python type, Series, or a mapping of column names to target dtypes. A mapping is useful when columns need different representations.
interview.followUp: What happens to unmapped columns? They remain unchanged, so the mapping need not mention every column.

interview.question: What does astype return, and how does it handle invalid data?
interview.answer: The method returns a DataFrame containing the converted data. By default, errors='raise', so invalid data for the requested dtype produces an exception rather than silently proceeding.
interview.followUp: When might errors='ignore' be useful? It can let a pipeline continue when conversion is opportunistic, though callers should verify the resulting dtypes.

keyPoints: DataFrame.astype converts the DataFrame to requested data types.
A single dtype applies one target type across the complete DataFrame.
A column-to-dtype mapping enables different target types for different columns.
The dtype parameter supports scalar dtype specifications and column mappings.
The errors parameter accepts raise or ignore and defaults to raise.
gotchas: With the default errors='raise', values that cannot be converted cause an exception; errors='ignore' suppresses that exception.

df.at.summary: `DataFrame.at` reads or writes one cell using a row-label and column-label pair. It is the label-based scalar counterpart to positional `iat`.
df.at.explanation: `DataFrame.at` provides scalar access using a row label and a column label. It supports both retrieval and assignment, making it suitable when exactly one cell is involved rather than a multi-cell selection.
df.at.returns: The value at the specified row/column label pair when reading; assignment updates that cell.

example.title: Read and update one labeled cell
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    [[0, 2, 3], [0, 4, 1], [10, 20, 30]],
    columns=["A", "B", "C"],
)

value = df.at[1, "B"]
df.at[1, "B"] = 10

assert value == 4
assert df.at[1, "B"] == 10
example.explanation: Use the label pair inside brackets to read one cell, or assign through the same expression to update it.

useCases.title: Scalar lookup
useCases.scenario: Read one known cell from a labeled table without selecting a larger slice.

useCases.title: Scalar update
useCases.scenario: Change one field identified by its row and column labels.

useCases.title: Series scalar access
useCases.scenario: Work with a Series obtained from a DataFrame row.

interview.question: What is `DataFrame.at` used for?
interview.answer: `at` performs label-based scalar access on a DataFrame. It can retrieve or assign one value identified by a row label and a column label.
interview.followUp: How would you access one cell by position instead of labels? Use `iat`, which provides integer-position-based scalar access.

interview.question: How does `at` differ from `loc`?
interview.answer: Both `at` and `loc` use labels, but `at` is intended for a single value. Use `loc` when selecting groups of rows or columns.
interview.followUp: What is the positional counterpart of `loc`? `iloc` selects by integer positions, while `iat` is the scalar positional counterpart.

interview.question: How do you update a single DataFrame cell with `at`?
interview.answer: Read with `df.at[row_label, column_label]` and assign with `df.at[row_label, column_label] = value`. The same labeled expression identifies the target cell in both cases.
interview.followUp: What happens if the requested label is absent during a read? A missing label causes `KeyError`.

keyPoints: Use `DataFrame.at` to address one cell through its row and column labels.
Its lookup semantics are label-based, like `loc`.
Choose it for scalar reads or writes rather than multi-cell selection.
A bracketed row/column pair returns the selected cell's value.
Assigning to the same indexer changes the selected cell.
gotchas: Reading a missing row or column label raises `KeyError`.
For a DataFrame, the indexer must represent a row/column pair, and each label must be scalar.

df.bfill.summary: DataFrame.bfill fills missing values by propagating the next valid observation backward along an axis. It can limit the number and position of values filled, or modify the DataFrame in place.
df.bfill.explanation: DataFrame.bfill replaces missing values by propagating the next non-missing observation backward along the selected axis. It returns a filled DataFrame unless inplace=True, in which case it modifies the object and returns None.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis along which to fill missing values: 0 or 'index', or 1 or 'columns'.

parameters.name: inplace
parameters.description: Whether to modify the DataFrame in place.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of consecutive missing values to fill; must be greater than zero when provided.

parameters.name: limit_area
parameters.description: Restricts filling to all positions, missing values inside valid values, or missing values outside valid values; requires limit.

df.bfill.returns: DataFrame or None. The filled DataFrame is returned unless inplace=True, which returns None.

example.title: Backward-fill limited gaps
example.code:
import pandas as pd

frame = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, None, 4], "b": [None, 2, None, 3]})
filled = frame.bfill(limit=1)
print(filled)
example.explanation: Creates a DataFrame and fills at most one consecutive missing value per gap using the next valid value.

useCases.title: Fill short time-series gaps
useCases.scenario: A time-ordered table has short gaps, and later observations are the appropriate values to propagate backward.

useCases.title: Fill interior gaps
useCases.scenario: Only interior missing runs should be completed while edge gaps remain missing.

useCases.title: Update in place
useCases.scenario: A pipeline requires controlled mutation of an existing DataFrame object.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.bfill do?
interview.answer: It performs backward filling: each missing value can receive the next valid observation later along the selected axis. By default, it operates on the index axis for a DataFrame.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent leading or trailing gaps from being filled? Set limit_area='inside' while also specifying limit.

interview.question: How does limit affect bfill?
interview.answer: limit restricts how many consecutive missing entries are filled. A gap longer than the limit is only partially filled, and a non-None limit must be greater than zero.
interview.followUp: How can you fill only missing values outside the valid-data region? Use limit_area='outside' with a specified limit.

interview.question: What does bfill return?
interview.answer: The method returns a DataFrame containing the filled values when inplace=False. With inplace=True, it modifies the original object and returns None.
interview.followUp: What alias-related concern follows from inplace=True? Other views, including no-copy column slices, may observe the mutation.

keyPoints: Use bfill when missing entries should inherit values from later observations rather than earlier ones.
The axis argument determines whether filling proceeds down rows or across columns.
Set inplace=True to mutate the existing DataFrame instead of receiving a separate result.
limit_area applies an inside or outside positional restriction, but only when limit is provided.
limit_area='outside' targets missing values beyond the valid observations at the ends.
gotchas: Using inplace=True can also change other views that reference the same DataFrame, such as a no-copy column slice.
When limit is supplied, it must be a positive integer.
With limit_area='inside', only missing values between valid observations are eligible for filling.

df.clip.summary: DataFrame.clip constrains values to optional lower and upper thresholds, replacing out-of-range entries with the relevant boundary. Scalar or array-like thresholds are supported.

import pandas as pd

primary = pd.DataFrame({"score": [10, None], "name": ["A", None]}, index=[1, 2])
fallback = pd.DataFrame({"score": [20, 30], "name": ["B", "C"]}, index=[2, 3])

interview.question: How does combine_first resolve overlapping values?
interview.answer: It fills missing values in the calling DataFrame with non-missing values from the other DataFrame at the same labels. Values already present in the caller take precedence when both frames contain non-missing values.
interview.followUp: What happens to the shape? The result uses the union of the two row indexes and column indexes, so it can contain rows or columns introduced by the other frame.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

original = pd.DataFrame({"score": [10, 20]})
copy = original.copy()
copy.loc[0, "score"] = 99

print(original.loc[0, "score"])  # 10
print(copy.loc[0, "score"])      # 99

interview.question: What is the default behavior of DataFrame.copy()?
interview.answer: copy() returns a new object containing copies of the caller's data and indices by default because deep defaults to True. Changes to the copied data or indices are therefore not reflected in the original.
interview.followUp: What does deep=True mean for objects stored in cells? It copies the container data but only copies references to nested Python objects, not those objects recursively.

interview.question: How does deep=False differ from the default?
interview.answer: deep=False creates a new DataFrame while copying neither the data nor the index; it copies references to them instead. The returned object still has the same type as its caller.
interview.followUp: How does Copy-on-Write alter shallow-copy behavior? A write to either object causes the affected data to be copied, preventing the other object from observing that mutation.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.copy() return?
interview.answer: The method returns a Series or DataFrame whose type matches the caller. For a DataFrame, this means copy() produces another DataFrame.

interview.followUp: How would you summarize non-numeric columns? Pass an appropriate dtype through include, such as include=["object"], so those columns are analyzed.

interview.question: How are percentiles selected?
interview.answer: By default, the percentile argument is None, which causes the method to include the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles. You can provide a list-like collection to request different percentile levels.
interview.followUp: What validation constraint applies to custom percentile values? Each value must fall between 0 and 1.

interview.question: How do include and exclude affect analysis?
interview.answer: The include and exclude arguments restrict the columns analyzed according to dtype. This lets a caller select non-numeric columns, omit particular dtype groups, or otherwise narrow the DataFrame summary.
interview.followUp: What happens if the filters select incompatible or overlapping dtype groups? The method validates the requested selection and may raise an error rather than producing an ambiguous summary.

The output characterizes distribution location, spread, and shape while leaving missing values out of calculations.
It supports numeric data, object data, and DataFrames containing mixed column types.
Leaving percentiles unset adds the first, second, and third quartiles.
The method accepts optional percentile, inclusion, and exclusion arguments.
The result contains summary statistics for the supplied data structure.
gotchas: Every value supplied in percentiles must be between 0 and 1.
Use include and exclude to control which DataFrame columns participate in the summary.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [10, 14, 11, 18]})
df["change"] = df["sales"].diff()

interview.question: What does DataFrame.diff() calculate by default?
interview.answer: It computes first discrete differences between DataFrame elements. With the defaults, each row is compared with the previous row, so the leading row has no earlier value to compare against.
interview.followUp: How would you compare adjacent columns instead? Pass axis=1, which takes differences across columns rather than rows.

interview.question: What is the purpose of periods?
interview.answer: periods controls the shift distance used for the comparison and defaults to 1. It also accepts negative values, allowing comparison in the opposite direction.
interview.followUp: What does periods=3 do? Each value is compared with the value three rows earlier when using the default axis.

interview.question: How does axis change the operation?
interview.answer: axis accepts 0 or 'index' for differences over rows, and 1 or 'columns' for differences over columns. The default is axis=0.
interview.followUp: What output type should callers expect? The method returns a DataFrame containing the first differences.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.drop do, and how does axis affect it?
interview.answer: It removes specified labels from rows or columns. The axis argument selects index labels with 0 or 'index', and column labels with 1 or 'columns'.
interview.followUp: How can the same operation be expressed without axis? Use index= for rows or columns= for columns; these are alternatives to labels combined with the corresponding axis.

interview.question: What does inplace change?
interview.answer: The default is inplace=False, so the method returns a DataFrame with the requested labels removed and leaves the original unchanged. With inplace=True, it modifies the object and returns None.
interview.followUp: When is inplace=True observable from the return value? The result is None, so callers must not assign it as though it were the modified DataFrame.

interview.question: How does drop work with a MultiIndex?
interview.answer: For a MultiIndex, level identifies the index level from which labels are removed. It can be an integer level position or a level name.
interview.followUp: Why specify level? It disambiguates removal in a multi-level index and avoids treating the label as a match across every level.

keyPoints: Use DataFrame.drop to remove selected row-index or column labels.

df.drop_duplicates.summary: Remove duplicate rows from a DataFrame, optionally judging duplicates by selected columns. Choose whether to keep the first, last, or none of each duplicate group, and optionally reset the result index.
df.drop_duplicates.explanation: The method identifies repeated rows using every column unless subset selects particular columns. It returns a deduplicated DataFrame by default; keep chooses the retained occurrence, ignore_index creates a fresh sequential index, and inplace changes the original object instead of returning a DataFrame.

parameters.name: subset
parameters.type: column label or iterable of labels, optional
parameters.description: Column label or iterable of labels used for identifying duplicates; if omitted, all columns are used.

parameters.name: keep
parameters.description: Which duplicate occurrence to retain: "first", "last", or False.

parameters.name: inplace
parameters.description: If True, modify the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one.

parameters.name: ignore_index
parameters.description: If True, use a new default integer index in the result.

df.drop_duplicates.returns: DataFrame or None: a DataFrame with duplicates removed, or None when inplace=True.

example.title: Remove repeated records
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "user": ["a", "a", "b"],
    "score": [10, 10, 8],
})

unique = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["user"], keep="first", ignore_index=True)
print(unique)
example.explanation: Keeps the first row for each user, considering only the user column, and rebuilds the result index.

interview.question: How does drop_duplicates decide which rows are duplicates?
interview.answer: By default, duplicate detection considers all columns and retains the first occurrence. Use subset to restrict the comparison to selected columns.
interview.followUp: How would you retain the latest record per key? Use subset for the key columns and keep="last", assuming the rows are already ordered by recency.

interview.question: What does the keep parameter control?
interview.answer: keep="first" retains the first duplicate occurrence, keep="last" retains the last, and keep=False removes every row belonging to a duplicate group.
interview.followUp: What happens when keep=False is used on a group appearing three times? All three rows are removed.

interview.question: What are the return behavior and index options?
interview.answer: The method returns a DataFrame containing duplicates removed, unless inplace=True, in which case it returns None. ignore_index=True makes the returned rows use a new default index.
interview.followUp: Why can relying on the old index be misleading after filtering? Removed rows leave gaps unless the index is explicitly rebuilt.

keyPoints: The method removes repeated rows and produces a deduplicated DataFrame by default.
Pass subset to define which columns participate in duplicate detection.
If subset is omitted, all columns are compared.
keep selects the representative row from each duplicate group.
keep="first" preserves the earliest occurrence in the current row order.
keep="last" preserves the final occurrence in the current row order.
keep=False removes every row that has a duplicate.
gotchas: Duplicate detection does not use the DataFrame index, including a time-based index.
With inplace=True, the operation mutates the DataFrame and returns None rather than a result DataFrame.

df.dropna.summary: DataFrame.dropna removes rows or columns containing missing values. Configure the axis, removal rule, minimum non-missing count, inspected labels, mutation behavior, and resulting index.
df.dropna.explanation: Call this DataFrame method to remove rows or columns containing missing values. By default it removes rows containing at least one missing value; use axis, how, thresh, subset, inplace, and ignore_index to control the operation.
df.dropna.syntax: DataFrame.dropna(*, axis=0, how=<no_default>, thresh=<no_default>, subset=None, inplace=False, ignore_index=False)

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis to inspect: 0 or 'index' for rows, or 1 or 'columns' for columns. Default: 0.

parameters.name: how
parameters.description: Remove an item if any or all considered values are missing. Default: 'any'.

parameters.name: thresh
parameters.description: Minimum number of non-missing values required.

parameters.name: subset
parameters.type: column label or iterable of labels, optional
parameters.description: Column or index labels on the other axis to inspect.

parameters.name: inplace
parameters.description: Modify the DataFrame in place instead of returning a new one. Default: False.

parameters.name: ignore_index
parameters.description: Relabel the resulting axis with a new default index. Default: False.

df.dropna.returns: A DataFrame with missing entries removed, or None when inplace=True.

example.title: Drop rows using selected columns
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ada", "Linus", "Grace"],
    "score": [95, None, 88],
    "note": [None, None, "ok"],
})

clean = df.dropna(subset=["score"])
print(clean)

complete = df.dropna(how="all", subset=["score", "note"])
print(complete)
example.explanation: The first call keeps rows with a score; the second removes rows whose selected fields are all missing.

interview.question: What does dropna do by default?
interview.answer: By default, dropna examines rows because axis defaults to 0. With how='any', a row is removed if at least one missing value is present; how='all' removes it only when every examined value is missing.
interview.followUp: How would you require a row to retain enough data? Use thresh with the required number of non-missing values, and do not combine it with how.

interview.question: How do axis and subset affect the operation?
interview.answer: axis=0 or 'index' removes rows, while axis=1 or 'columns' removes columns. The selected axis determines whether the missing-value test is applied to row entries or column entries.
interview.followUp: How can the test be limited to particular fields when removing rows? Pass those column labels through subset.

interview.question: When should thresh or ignore_index be used?
interview.answer: thresh specifies the minimum number of non-NA values required. For row removal, subset can restrict which columns are considered; ignore_index=True makes the resulting axis use a new default integer index.
interview.followUp: What happens when inplace=True? The DataFrame is modified directly and the return value is None.

keyPoints: The method filters missing entries from a DataFrame along a chosen axis.
With axis=0 or 'index', the operation removes rows that meet the selected missing-value rule.
With axis=1 or 'columns', it removes columns that meet the selected rule.
how='any' removes an axis item when at least one considered value is missing.
how='all' removes an axis item only when all considered values are missing.
thresh sets the minimum count of non-missing values an axis item must have to remain.
subset supplies labels on the other axis that limit which values participate in the missingness check.
ignore_index controls whether the resulting axis keeps its original labels or is relabeled with a default index.
gotchas: Do not pass thresh together with how; choose either a minimum non-missing count or an any/all rule.
Select one axis per call: rows or columns, rather than attempting to drop along both axes at once.
When inplace=True, use the original DataFrame and do not expect the method to return the cleaned DataFrame.

frame = pd.DataFrame({

print(frame.dtypes)

interview.question: What does DataFrame.dtypes return?
interview.answer: DataFrame.dtypes is a property, so it is accessed without parentheses. It returns a pandas Series whose values are the dtypes of the DataFrame’s columns and whose index is the original column index.
interview.followUp: How would you use the result to select columns by type? Use DataFrame.select_dtypes, which filters columns according to include and exclude dtype criteria.

interview.question: How is the returned Series aligned with the DataFrame?
interview.answer: Each output Series entry corresponds to one DataFrame column. The Series index contains the DataFrame’s original column labels, while its values describe the respective column types.
interview.followUp: What happens when a column contains mixed types? The documentation says such columns are stored with the object dtype.

interview.question: Why inspect DataFrame.dtypes before transforming data?
interview.answer: It is useful for examining a heterogeneous table before type-dependent processing, such as identifying numeric, temporal, or object-typed columns. It reports the inferred or assigned dtype currently held by each column.
interview.followUp: How can types be changed? DataFrame.astype casts a pandas object to a specified dtype, while DataFrame.convert_dtypes converts columns to suitable dtypes supporting pd.NA.

The result is a pandas Series rather than a scalar or mapping.
Column labels become the index of the returned Series, preserving their correspondence.
The Series values describe individual column dtypes, such as integer, floating-point, datetime, or string types.
Series.dtypes is a related reference for inspecting the dtype object underlying a Series.
gotchas: A column containing mixed Python value types is represented with the object dtype, so object does not necessarily mean the values are strings.

df.duplicated.summary: Returns a boolean Series identifying duplicate DataFrame rows. Compare all columns by default, or specify subset columns and choose whether to preserve the first, last, or none of each duplicate group.
df.duplicated.explanation: Call this method to obtain a boolean Series aligned with the DataFrame index. Duplicate status is determined across all columns unless subset narrows the comparison, and keep controls which occurrence remains unmarked.

parameters.name: subset
parameters.type: label or iterable of labels, optional
parameters.description: Column label or iterable of labels used for duplicate detection; if omitted, all columns are considered.

parameters.name: keep
parameters.description: Controls which duplicate occurrences are marked: 'first', 'last', or False. Defaults to 'first'.

df.duplicated.returns: A boolean Series indicating whether each row is duplicated according to keep.

example.title: Detect duplicate rows
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "brand": ["A", "A", "B", "B"],
    "model": ["x", "x", "y", "z"],
})

print(df.duplicated())
print(df.duplicated(subset=["brand"], keep=False))
example.explanation: The first call checks complete rows, while the second checks only brand values and marks every member of each duplicate group.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.duplicated return?
interview.answer: It returns a boolean Series with one value per DataFrame row. A True value means that row is considered duplicated under the selected subset and keep policy.
interview.followUp: How would you identify all rows involved in duplication? Use df.duplicated(keep=False), which marks every occurrence in each duplicated group.

interview.question: How does subset change duplicate detection?
interview.answer: If subset is omitted, all columns participate in duplicate detection. If supplied, it can be one column label or an iterable of labels, so only those columns determine equality.
interview.followUp: How can you detect duplicate business keys while retaining other columns? Pass the key columns through subset, then use the resulting mask to select or inspect full rows.

interview.question: Explain the keep parameter.
interview.answer: keep accepts 'first', 'last', or False and defaults to 'first'. The first option flags all but the first occurrence, the second flags all but the last, and False flags every occurrence.
interview.followUp: When is keep='last' useful? It is useful when the final record should be retained as the representative and earlier matching records should be identified.

keyPoints: The method produces a boolean Series that identifies duplicate rows without modifying the DataFrame.
A row is duplicated when the compared column values recur in another row.
You can compare complete rows or restrict detection to selected columns.
subset selects the columns used for comparison; omitting it uses every column.
keep controls which occurrence of each duplicate group is marked True.
gotchas: The default keep='first' leaves the first row in each duplicate group unmarked and flags later matches.
With keep='last', the final row in each duplicate group is unmarked instead of the first.
Using keep=False flags every row belonging to a duplicated group, including its first and last occurrences.

import pandas as pd

scores = pd.DataFrame({"math": [80, 90], "bonus": [5, 3]})
scores.eval("total = math + bonus", inplace=True)

interview.question: What does DataFrame.eval do?
interview.answer: It evaluates a string in the context of the DataFrame’s columns, so column names can be used directly without prefixing them with the DataFrame variable. An assignment expression can derive or replace a column.
interview.followUp: How would you reference an external Python variable? Prefix that variable with @ in the expression, such as @threshold.

interview.question: How does inplace affect the result?
interview.answer: With inplace=False, the default, an assignment produces a new DataFrame and leaves the original unchanged. With inplace=True, an assignment mutates the existing DataFrame and the method returns None.
interview.followUp: What should code inspect when inplace=True? It should use the mutated DataFrame rather than expecting a returned result.

interview.question: How are unusual column names handled?
interview.answer: The expression may refer to columns whose names are not valid Python identifiers by surrounding those names with backticks. This covers names containing spaces, punctuation other than underscores, or leading digits.
interview.followUp: Can a column named like a Python keyword be referenced with backticks? No; the documentation says Python-keyword column names cannot be used.

df.ewm.explanation: Calling `ewm` creates an exponentially weighted window over the DataFrame. Choose one decay specification, then call a window operation such as `mean()`; `adjust`, missing-value handling, minimum observations, time-based decay, and execution method control the calculation.

parameters.name: span

parameters.name: alpha

parameters.name: adjust
parameters.description: Whether to use the decaying adjustment factor; default True.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"price": [10, 12, 11, 15]})
result = df.ewm(span=3, adjust=False).mean()
print(result)
