interview.question: What does DataFrame.unstack do?
interview.answer: It pivots selected index levels onto the columns axis. For a MultiIndex, the result is a DataFrame whose innermost column level contains the pivoted labels.
interview.followUp: What happens with a non-MultiIndex? It returns a Series, which is the analogous result when there is no hierarchical index to expand.

interview.question: How is the level selected?
interview.answer: level identifies the index level or levels to move and accepts an integer, a level name, or a list of either. Its default is -1, meaning the last index level.
interview.followUp: How would you select a level robustly when index order may change? Give the level a stable name and pass that name rather than relying on its numeric position.

interview.question: What do fill_value and sort control?
interview.answer: fill_value supplies a replacement for missing values created by the reshape, while sort controls ordering of the resulting MultiIndex columns and defaults to True. Setting sort=False retains first-appearance ordering for the relevant result ordering.
interview.followUp: When should fill_value be avoided? Avoid it when missingness carries meaning or when the replacement value would force an unsuitable interpretation of the data.

keyPoints: The operation moves selected index levels into the column axis.
For a MultiIndex input, the reshaped result is a DataFrame with an added column level.
The labels from the moved index level become the innermost column labels.
level accepts a position, a level name, or multiple such selectors; it defaults to the final index level.
fill_value can provide one scalar replacement for cells introduced as missing by unstacking.
sort is Boolean and defaults to True for ordering the resulting MultiIndex columns.
gotchas: A regular single-level index produces a Series rather than a DataFrame.

df.update.summary: DataFrame.update mutates a DataFrame with aligned, non-missing values from another object. It preserves the target’s shape and can either overwrite populated cells or fill only missing ones.
df.update.explanation: DataFrame.update aligns another DataFrame by index and column labels, then mutates the original object with eligible non-missing values. By default, incoming values replace existing ones; options can restrict updates to missing cells, filter candidates, or raise on overlapping non-missing data.

parameters.name: other
parameters.type: DataFrame or object coercible into a DataFrame
parameters.description: DataFrame or object coercible into a DataFrame; a Series must have a name used as its column label for alignment.

parameters.name: join
parameters.description: Only 'left' is implemented; preserves the target's index and columns.

parameters.name: overwrite
parameters.description: Controls whether aligned non-NA incoming values replace existing target values; false updates only target NA values.

parameters.name: filter_func
parameters.description: Callable receiving a one-dimensional array and returning a boolean one-dimensional array; True marks values to update.

parameters.name: errors
parameters.description: Controls conflicts where both objects have non-NA overlapping data; 'raise' raises ValueError.

df.update.returns: None; the DataFrame is modified in place.

example.title: Update matching values in place
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [400, 500, 600]})
updates = pd.DataFrame({"B": [4, 5, 6], "C": [7, 8, 9]})
df.update(updates)
print(df)
example.explanation: The matching B values are changed in place; the unmatched C column is not added.

useCases.title: Missing-value filling

interview.question: What does DataFrame.update do?
interview.answer: It aligns the other object on row and column labels and updates the target in place with non-missing incoming values. The target keeps its original shape, so unmatched labels do not add rows or columns.
interview.followUp: How would you update only missing target cells? Use overwrite=False, which limits changes to positions where the original DataFrame is NA.

interview.question: How do overwrite and filter_func affect updates?
interview.answer: With overwrite=True, overlapping non-missing values from other replace target values. With overwrite=False, only target cells that are missing are eligible for replacement.
interview.followUp: Can non-missing target values still be changed when overwrite=False? Yes, a filter_func can select values to update, including values other than NA.

interview.question: When should errors='raise' be used?
interview.answer: errors='ignore' is the default and permits overlapping non-NA values to be replaced according to the update rules. errors='raise' instead raises ValueError when both objects contain non-missing data at an overlapping position.
interview.followUp: What shape-changing join can update perform? None: only a left join is implemented, preserving the original index and columns.

keyPoints: The target DataFrame is mutated directly, using non-missing values from the supplied object.
The source should share at least one row or column label with the target so alignment can locate update positions.
The default overwrite=True replaces existing target values where aligned incoming values are non-missing.
Setting overwrite=False makes updates fill missing target cells rather than replace populated ones.
filter_func allows a callable to select update positions beyond the usual missing-value cases.
Updating preserves the target's row count; incoming rows outside the target's labels are not appended.
gotchas: The operation cannot expand the target's index or columns: join only accepts the left-join behavior, so unmatched labels from the other object are ignored.
A Series input needs a name because that name supplies the column label used for alignment.
The method mutates the target and returns None; do not assign its result as the updated DataFrame.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Sort by frequencies when True.

interview.question: What does DataFrame.value_counts return?
interview.answer: It returns a Series whose index represents each distinct row combination and whose values are their frequencies. With subset, only the specified columns define the combinations.
interview.followUp: What changes when normalize=True? It returns proportions rather than counts, so the values represent each combination's share of the counted rows.

interview.question: How does subset affect the result?
interview.answer: subset selects the columns used to form unique combinations; if omitted, every DataFrame column participates. The result therefore distinguishes rows by the selected columns rather than necessarily by complete rows.
interview.followUp: What index structure should be expected for multiple selected columns? The result uses a MultiIndex with one level for each input column.

interview.question: How do normalize, sort, and ascending change the output?
interview.answer: normalize=False produces frequencies, while normalize=True produces proportions. sort controls whether results are ordered by frequency, and ascending controls the direction when sorting by frequency.
interview.followUp: How can missing-value rows be counted? Set dropna=False so rows containing NA values are included.

keyPoints: The method returns a Series with one entry for each distinct row pattern.
Distinct combinations form the result index, allowing each frequency to be associated with its row values.
Use subset to restrict counting to selected columns instead of the entire DataFrame.
normalize=True changes the output from integer-like frequencies to relative proportions.
sort=True orders results according to their frequencies; setting it to False disables frequency sorting.
ascending=True reverses the usual descending frequency order when sorting is enabled.
gotchas: Missing values are excluded unless dropna=False; a row with an NA in any counted column is omitted by default.
The default output places the most frequent combinations first; use ascending=True to reverse the frequency order.

df.values.summary: `DataFrame.values` exposes a DataFrame's cell data as a NumPy array without index or column labels. Prefer `DataFrame.to_numpy()` for new code.
df.values.explanation: Accessing `DataFrame.values` produces a NumPy array containing the DataFrame's cell values and removes both axes labels. Prefer `DataFrame.to_numpy()` when you need explicit control over dtype, copying, or missing-value representation.
df.values.returns: numpy.ndarray — the values of the DataFrame.

example.title: Extract unlabeled values
example.code:
import pandas as pd

frame = pd.DataFrame({"age": [3, 29], "height": [94, 170]})
values = frame.values
print(values)
print(values.shape)
example.explanation: The property returns the data as a NumPy array, without the DataFrame's index or column labels.

useCases.title: NumPy interoperability
useCases.scenario: Pass a table's raw values to NumPy-based code that does not need pandas labels.

useCases.title: Quick data inspection

useCases.title: Array-oriented processing
useCases.scenario: Obtain a compact two-dimensional array for homogeneous tabular data.

interview.question: What does `DataFrame.values` return?
interview.answer: `DataFrame.values` is a property that returns a NumPy representation of the DataFrame. It contains the cell values only; the index and column labels are omitted.
interview.followUp: What happens with mixed column dtypes? The result uses a common accommodating dtype, so values may be implicitly upcast; for example, compatible numeric types can produce a broader numeric dtype.

interview.question: How are labels and dtypes handled?
interview.answer: The returned array has rows and columns corresponding to the DataFrame's rows and columns, but it has no pandas axis labels. Its dtype is determined by the values across the columns rather than necessarily preserving each column's dtype.
interview.followUp: Why can a mixed-type frame yield an object array? A single NumPy array needs one dtype, so heterogeneous values may require the broadest type that can represent them.

interview.question: What should new code use instead of `DataFrame.values`?
interview.answer: The documentation recommends `DataFrame.to_numpy()` instead of `.values`. `to_numpy()` is the explicit API for converting to a NumPy array and is the preferred modern alternative.
interview.followUp: When should a developer avoid conversion entirely? When labels or pandas semantics are needed, keep the DataFrame and use pandas indexing or transformation methods instead.

keyPoints: The property converts the DataFrame's tabular data into a NumPy array.
The output contains cell values but excludes both the index and column labels.
The return value is a `numpy.ndarray` containing the DataFrame data.
When columns have different dtypes, pandas chooses a common dtype capable of representing all values.
A numeric example of implicit promotion is a frame mixing `float16` and `float32`, which yields `float32` output.

Mixed column dtypes can cause the returned array to be implicitly upcast to a common dtype, potentially changing how values are represented.

import pandas as pd

interview.answer: `Series.dt` is a dtype-specific namespace for datetimelike Series. It exposes datetime, timedelta, and period properties and operations such as month extraction and formatting.
interview.followUp: What should be done when the source values are strings? Convert valid strings with `pd.to_datetime` before using `dt`.

interview.question: What is pandas.Index, and what input does it accept?
interview.answer: pandas.Index is an immutable sequence used for indexing and alignment, and it stores axis labels for pandas objects. It can be constructed from one-dimensional array-like input such as a list, NumPy array, or Series.
interview.followUp: How does tupleize_cols affect construction? When true, pandas attempts to create a MultiIndex when the input makes that possible.

interview.question: What are the main constructor parameters?
interview.answer: The data argument supplies one-dimensional array-like labels. dtype can request the output dtype, name stores an index name, copy controls whether the input is copied, and tupleize_cols controls possible MultiIndex creation.
interview.followUp: What happens if dtype is omitted? pandas infers the dtype from the supplied data.

interview.question: What constraints apply to Index values?
interview.answer: Index objects are immutable and require hashable elements, which makes them suitable for stable axis labels and alignment. They support numeric dtypes broadly, except that numpy.float16 cannot be held.
interview.followUp: Can an Index contain mutable Python objects? No; mutable objects are not hashable and therefore cannot be Index elements.

interview.question: What is a MultiIndex?
interview.answer: A MultiIndex is a hierarchical index whose labels have multiple levels. It can be viewed as an array of unique tuples, so a single axis can represent combinations such as region and team.
interview.followUp: How can you construct one without manually supplying levels and codes? Use class methods such as from_arrays, from_tuples, from_product, or from_frame.

interview.question: What do levels and codes represent?
interview.answer: The levels argument contains the unique labels for each level. The codes argument contains integer arrays that identify which label from each level is used at every position.
interview.followUp: Why are codes integers rather than labels? They provide positional references into the unique label arrays stored in levels.

interview.question: When would you use MultiIndex.from_product?

interview.answer: `pd.Period` represents a span of time, while `Timestamp` represents one instant. The `freq` argument defines the span's granularity, such as monthly, quarterly, or yearly.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain an instant from a Period? Use `to_timestamp`, selecting an appropriate frequency and optionally the start or end with `how`.

interview.question: What are the main inputs to `pd.Period`?
interview.answer: The `value` identifies the time period and may be a Period, string, datetime, date, or pandas Timestamp. `freq` accepts a pandas period frequency string or corresponding frequency object.
interview.followUp: What happens when `value` is a datetime but `freq` is omitted? Construction cannot determine the intended period frequency, so `freq` is required.

interview.question: How do you change a Period's frequency?
interview.answer: `asfreq` converts a Period to another frequency and lets you choose the start or end of the interval. For example, a monthly Period can be represented as a daily Period at its start.
interview.followUp: Why might conversion to a finer frequency need an endpoint choice? A broader interval contains multiple finer-grained periods, so `how` selects which boundary-relative period represents it.

An `ordinal` can identify the period by its offset from the proleptic Gregorian epoch.
Use `asfreq` to change frequency while choosing the interval's start or end.

interview.question: What does `pd.Timedelta` represent?

interview.followUp: How can an integer be interpreted correctly? Supply `unit`, because the unit argument denotes the unit of an integer input and defaults to nanoseconds.

interview.question: Which kinds of input can construct a Timedelta?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts duration-like values such as `Timedelta`, `timedelta`, `np.timedelta64`, strings, and integers. It also accepts keyword components including days, seconds, microseconds, milliseconds, minutes, hours, and weeks.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to numeric construction? A numeric value should be paired with `unit` so its scale is explicit rather than relying on the default.

interview.question: What unit does the `.value` representation use?
interview.answer: The `.value` attribute exposes the duration's underlying integer representation in nanoseconds. Even when another input unit is supplied, this stored value is expressed in nanoseconds.
interview.followUp: What happens to finer-than-nanosecond input? Its precision is truncated to nanoseconds.

interview.question: What is `pandas.Timestamp` used for?
interview.answer: `Timestamp` is pandas’ replacement for Python’s `datetime.datetime` and is generally interchangeable with it. It is also the element type used by `DatetimeIndex` and other time-series-oriented pandas structures.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful in a DataFrame? A consistent timestamp type enables pandas time-series indexing and datetime-aware operations across columns and indexes.

interview.question: How does `Timestamp` interpret numeric input?
interview.answer: The primary constructor accepts a datetime-like value, string, integer, or float through `ts_input`. Numeric values can be interpreted with `unit`, whose supported values include days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, and nanoseconds.
interview.followUp: What does `Timestamp(1513393355.5, unit='s')` represent? It interprets the number as seconds from the Unix epoch, including its fractional part.

interview.question: What constructor conventions does `Timestamp` provide?
interview.answer: The constructor supports three calling conventions. The primary form accepts four parameters, while the other two mirror `datetime.datetime`; arguments may be positional or keyword arguments, but positional and keyword styles must not be mixed in those forms.
interview.followUp: How would you represent timezone information? Supply `tz` for the timestamp timezone, or use `tzinfo` in the datetime-style form as documented.

interview.followUp: What happens to a Series? The result remains a Series; otherwise the result is an ndarray.

interview.question: How do you handle values that cannot be parsed?
interview.answer: errors="raise" throws for invalid parsing, whereas errors="coerce" replaces invalid values with NaN. The default is "raise".
interview.followUp: How can invalid values be handled without silently ignoring them? Catch the conversion exception explicitly rather than using the deprecated ignore option.

interview.question: What is the purpose of downcast and dtype_backend?
interview.answer: downcast accepts integer, signed, unsigned, or float and requests a smaller compatible dtype. It does not force an unsafe conversion when the values cannot fit.
interview.followUp: What additional output choice is available? dtype_backend can select the nullable data representation, including nullable output for coerced values.

keyPoints: Use the function to parse input values into numeric data.
Without downcasting, non-numeric input generally produces float64 or int64 according to the parsed data.
Set downcast when a smaller integer, unsigned integer, signed integer, or floating-point dtype is desirable.
The argument may be a scalar, sequence, one-dimensional array, or Series.
Coercion converts unparseable entries into NaN instead of stopping the operation.
The output type follows the input category rather than always being a Series.
gotchas: The default error policy raises when any value cannot be parsed; use errors="coerce" when invalid values should become missing.
Very large numbers may lose precision during conversion.

pd.wide_to_long.summary: Unpivot a DataFrame whose measured columns share stub prefixes and suffixes. Identifier columns become part of the resulting index, while the extracted suffix is named by j.
pd.wide_to_long.explanation: Provide the wide DataFrame, stub names for column groups, identifier columns, and the name for the extracted suffix. Matching columns such as A_2023 and A_2024 are reshaped into an A column indexed by the identifiers and the suffix; other columns remain unchanged.
pd.wide_to_long.syntax: pandas.wide_to_long(df, stubnames, i, j, sep='', suffix='\d+')

parameters.name: df
parameters.description: The wide-format DataFrame.

parameters.name: stubnames
parameters.description: The stub name or names; wide variables are assumed to start with them.

parameters.name: i
parameters.description: Column or columns used as identifier variables.

parameters.name: j
parameters.description: Name of the sub-observation variable in the long format.

parameters.name: sep
parameters.description: Separator in wide column names to strip from long-format names; default is an empty string.

parameters.name: suffix
parameters.description: Regular expression capturing the desired suffixes; default is '\d+'.

pd.wide_to_long.returns: DataFrame containing each stub name as a variable, with a new index formed from (i, j).

example.title: Convert year-suffixed columns to long format
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": [1, 2],
    "A_2023": [10, 20],
    "A_2024": [11, 21],
})

long = pd.wide_to_long(df, stubnames="A", i="id", j="year", sep="_")
print(long.reset_index())
example.explanation: The identifier column remains an index level, while matching A_year columns become one A value column and a year sub-observation column.

useCases.scenario: Reshape several parallel groups such as A_2023 and B_2023 together.

interview.question: What does pandas.wide_to_long do?
interview.answer: It reshapes columns grouped by a shared stub and suffix into a long DataFrame. The supplied i columns identify rows, while j names the extracted suffix level.
interview.followUp: How would you handle columns such as A-2023? Pass sep="-" so the separator is removed when forming the long-format names.

interview.question: How do stubnames, i, and j control the reshape?
interview.answer: stubnames identifies the prefixes of measured-column groups, i supplies identifier columns, and j names the sub-observation variable. For example, stubnames="A" matches A1 and A2 with the default separator and suffix rules.
interview.followUp: How can multiple measured groups be reshaped together? Supply a list-like stubnames value, such as ["A", "B"].

interview.question: When should sep or suffix be changed?
interview.answer: sep specifies the separator between a stub and suffix and is stripped from long-format names. suffix is a regular expression for accepted suffixes; the default \d+ selects numeric suffixes.
interview.followUp: What pattern selects nonnumeric suffixes? Use a negated digit class such as \D+ when the suffixes contain no numbers.

keyPoints: Use the function to turn repeated suffix-based columns into rows in a long-format DataFrame.
It is a convenient alternative to melt when the column groups follow a predictable stub-and-suffix layout.
Each stub name acts as the prefix used to discover its corresponding wide-format columns.
The i argument identifies columns that distinguish the original observations and become index levels.
The j argument names the index level holding each extracted suffix.
Columns not matched as stub-and-suffix measurements are retained in the result.
gotchas: The default suffix pattern is numeric; use a regular expression such as \D+ when suffixes contain no numbers.
Numeric suffixes are converted to numeric index values, so the j level may not remain text.

pivot_table.summary: Creates a spreadsheet-style pivot table from a DataFrame by grouping row and column keys and aggregating selected values. It supports custom aggregation, missing-value filling, totals, categorical-group control, and sorting.
pivot_table.explanation: Use pandas.pivot_table to group a DataFrame by row and column keys while aggregating one or more value columns. The result is a DataFrame whose row and column levels can be MultiIndex objects, with options for missing-value filling, totals, sorting, and categorical-group handling.
pivot_table.syntax: pandas.pivot_table(data, values=None, index=None, columns=None, aggfunc='mean', fill_value=None, margins=False, dropna=True, margins_name='All', observed=True, sort=True, **kwargs)

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Input pandas DataFrame object.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Column or columns to aggregate.

parameters.name: index
parameters.type: column, Grouper, array, or sequence of the previous
parameters.description: Keys to group by on the pivot table index.

parameters.name: columns
parameters.type: column, Grouper, array, or sequence of the previous
parameters.description: Keys to group by on the pivot table column.

parameters.name: aggfunc
parameters.type: function, list of functions, dict, default 'mean'
parameters.description: Function, list of functions, or dictionary used for aggregation; default is mean.

parameters.name: fill_value
parameters.description: Value used to replace missing values in the result after aggregation.

parameters.name: margins
parameters.description: Whether to add partial aggregates; default is False.

parameters.name: dropna
parameters.description: Whether to exclude missing values from group keys; default is True.

parameters.name: margins_name
parameters.description: Label for the totals row and column; default is 'All'.

parameters.name: observed
parameters.description: Whether to show only observed categorical groups; default is True.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Whether to sort the result; default is True.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.description: Additional keyword arguments.

example.title: Aggregate sales into a pivot table
example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "region": ["East", "East", "West"],
    "product": ["A", "B", "A"],
    "sales": [10, 20, 15],
})

result = pd.pivot_table(
    df,
    values="sales",
    index="region",
    columns="product",
    aggfunc="sum",
    fill_value=0,
)
print(result)
example.explanation: Groups sales by region and product, sums each group, and replaces missing combinations with zero.

interview.question: What does pandas.pivot_table do?
interview.answer: It creates a spreadsheet-style pivot table as a DataFrame. The supplied index and columns keys define groups, and aggfunc computes the aggregate for the selected values.
interview.followUp: What structure can the result have? Its row and column levels are stored in MultiIndex objects when the grouping produces multiple levels.

interview.question: How does aggfunc work?
interview.answer: aggfunc defaults to 'mean'. It can also be a function, a list of functions, or a dictionary mapping columns to aggregation functions.
interview.followUp: What happens with a function list? The resulting columns become hierarchical, with top-level labels inferred from the function names.

interview.question: How do you add totals and handle missing combinations?
interview.answer: margins=True adds partial aggregates across categories, using the margins_name label, which defaults to 'All'. fill_value can replace missing cells after aggregation.
interview.followUp: Can grouping keys be non-column arrays? Yes; index and columns accept arrays or sequences, subject to the documented grouping requirements.

keyPoints: The function returns a DataFrame arranged like a spreadsheet pivot table.
Grouped row or column dimensions can be represented by hierarchical MultiIndex levels.
values selects the column or columns whose data will be aggregated.
index defines the grouping keys for result rows.
columns defines the grouping keys for result columns.
A dictionary aggfunc lets each aggregated column use its own function or list of functions.
gotchas: Supplying multiple aggregation functions creates hierarchical result columns, which can change how columns must be selected.
With categorical groupers, observed controls whether only observed combinations or all category combinations appear.
fill_value replaces missing values in the aggregated result; it does not change missing values before aggregation.

interview.question: What does pandas.read_json do and what does it return?
interview.answer: read_json accepts a JSON string, path, or file-like input and converts it to a pandas object. By default, typ is frame, so tabular input normally produces a DataFrame.
interview.followUp: How would you process a large newline-delimited JSON file? Use lines=True and set chunksize to obtain a JsonReader instead of loading all records at once.

interview.question: Why is the orient parameter important?
interview.answer: orient tells pandas which JSON layout to expect, such as records, index, columns, split, values, or table. The selected layout determines how keys, indexes, and columns are reconstructed.
interview.followUp: How would you read an object keyed by row labels? Choose orient="index", optionally supplying columns when the JSON values are record-like.

interview.question: How do lines and chunksize support streaming-style ingestion?
interview.answer: With lines=True, pandas reads line-delimited JSON, where each line represents a separate JSON object. With chunksize set, the function returns a JsonReader for iterative consumption.
interview.followUp: What memory behavior should be expected without chunksize? The function loads the result as a Series or DataFrame rather than exposing a batch iterator.

keyPoints: read_json converts JSON text into a pandas object.
The input can be a JSON file or JSON-like source, not only an in-memory string.
The function handles line-delimited and compressed inputs as well as multiple JSON orientations.
A string path is a supported input form.
Supported URL schemes include HTTP, FTP, S3, and file URLs.
Providing a nonzero chunksize returns a JsonReader for incremental processing.
gotchas: Setting chunksize changes the result from an eagerly loaded pandas object to an iterator, so consume it in batches.
A string input may be treated as a URL, so distinguish URL-like sources from local paths when constructing inputs.

Series.summary: pandas.Series is a one-dimensional labeled data structure that supports positional and label-based indexing. Arithmetic aligns operands by their index labels.
Series.explanation: Series stores one-dimensional data together with an index and optional name. It supports label-based and integer-based access, while arithmetic with another Series matches values by index and produces the sorted union of their indexes.

parameters.name: data
parameters.type: array-like, Iterable, dict, or scalar value
parameters.description: Array-like, Iterable, dict, or scalar value containing the Series data.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: Array-like or Index labels; labels must be hashable and match the data length.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Output data type; inferred from data when omitted.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Name assigned to the Series.

parameters.name: copy
parameters.description: Whether to copy the input data.

Series.returns: A pandas Series object containing the supplied data, index, dtype, and name.

example.title: Create and align Series values
example.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["a", "b", "c"], name="scores")
print(s.loc["b"])
print((s + pd.Series([1, 2], index=["b", "c"])).dropna())
example.explanation: Creates a labeled Series, selects by label, and demonstrates index-aligned arithmetic.

useCases.scenario: Work with timestamps and indexed observations in a time-series workflow.

useCases.scenario: Combine or compare labeled values from different sources while preserving label correspondence.

interview.question: What is a pandas Series?
interview.answer: Series is a one-dimensional ndarray-like object with axis labels. It supports both integer-based and label-based indexing and includes methods for operations involving its index.
interview.followUp: How does Series arithmetic handle different indexes? It aligns operands by their associated index values rather than by array position.

interview.question: What are the main Series constructor inputs?
interview.answer: The data argument supplies the stored values and may be array-like, iterable, a dictionary, or a scalar. The index argument supplies labels; without one, pandas uses a RangeIndex.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to an explicit index? Its values must be hashable and have the same length as the data.

interview.question: How does pandas align two Series during arithmetic?
interview.answer: Series operations such as addition align values using their associated indexes, even when the operands have different lengths. The output index is the sorted union of both input indexes.
interview.followUp: What should be checked after alignment? Labels missing from either operand can produce missing results, so inspect or handle those values explicitly.

keyPoints: Series represents one-dimensional labeled data and can also model time-series values.
Values can be selected using positional indexing or index labels.
Its API includes many methods that operate with or transform the Series index.
Arithmetic matches values by labels instead of assuming equal positional layouts.
The constructor's data input is the content from which the Series is created.
When dtype is omitted, pandas infers the output data type from the supplied data.
gotchas: Index labels may repeat, but every label must be hashable.
An explicitly supplied index must contain hashable values and match the data length.
Operations between Series can add labels that were absent from one input, because their indexes are unioned and sorted.

str accessor.summary: Pandas' `.str` accessor supplies vectorized string operations for Series and Index objects, including DataFrame columns and labels. Use it for tasks such as trimming, changing case, matching patterns, splitting, extracting, and concatenating text.
str accessor.explanation: The `.str` accessor exposes vectorized string operations for a pandas Series and can also be used with DataFrame column labels because `df.columns` is an Index. Accessor methods transform or inspect string elements while preserving pandas alignment and missing-value handling.
str accessor.returns: A pandas Series, Index, or DataFrame depending on the selected object and operation; shape and values are determined by the specific `.str` method.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": [" Alice ", "Bob"]})
df["name"] = df["name"].str.strip().str.lower()
print(df)
example.explanation: Cleans a string column by chaining the accessor's elementwise methods.

interview.question: What is the purpose of pandas' `.str` accessor?
interview.answer: The `.str` accessor provides vectorized string operations on pandas Series and related Index objects. It lets code apply methods such as `strip`, `lower`, `contains`, and `rsplit` element by element without an explicit Python loop.
interview.followUp: What happens when the data is not string-like? The accessor is intended primarily for strings, and unsupported non-string uses may fail or remain unsupported.

interview.question: How would you use `.str` with a DataFrame?
interview.answer: A DataFrame column is normally selected as a Series, so `df["column"].str.method(...)` applies a string operation to each value. The accessor can also operate on `df.columns`, because the columns object is an Index.
interview.followUp: How can multiple transformations be composed? Chain accessor calls, such as `.str.strip().str.lower()`, when each stage returns compatible string-like data.

interview.question: What kinds of operations does the accessor provide?
interview.answer: The accessor supports operations including concatenation, splitting, extraction, containment checks, and case or whitespace transformations. Methods that split or extract can change the result shape, for example by producing multiple columns or a DataFrame.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when using regex-oriented methods? Verify whether the method interprets its pattern as a regular expression and choose arguments accordingly.

keyPoints: Prefer pandas' dedicated string dtype when creating or normalizing text columns.
The accessor is available for cleaning or transforming column labels as well as Series values.
Use `cat` to combine string values according to its documented options.
Use `contains` to produce elementwise boolean matches for a pattern or regular expression.
Use `rsplit` when the meaningful delimiter is nearest the right-hand end of each value.
gotchas: Use it with string-like data; operations on unsupported element types are not generally supported.
Position-based string indexing beyond an element's length produces a missing value rather than an exception.
A Series containing list elements cannot use the string methods designed for string elements.
